newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG army chief calls on Chan to quit over mercenaries.
newsitem.headline: PNG army chief calls on Chan to quit over mercenaries.

text.p: Papua New Guinea's army chief gave Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan a 48-hour deadline to quit on Monday, saying he would not accept a "quick-fix" plan to use foreign mercenaries to end the war on Bougainville island.

But Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok, commander of the PNG Defence Force, said he was not staging a coup and remained committed to democracy in the South Pacific nation. "If the PM and his deputy and minister for defence do not step down within 48 hours then I will plea to Papua New Guineans to join hands to force them to resign," Singirok said in an "Address to the Nation" handed out to journalists.
Eyewitnesses said Port Moresby remained calm and a senior army official, Colonel Jack Tuat, told Reuters that all troops in the capital were still in their barracks.

Papua New Guinea, which has a population of 4.3 million mainly Melanesians, has 3,400 defence force troops and 4,600 para-military police, including riot squads used to put down frequent tribal fighting.

PNG's latest crisis has been sparked by Chan's decision to hire expensive foreign mercenaries to train and equip the defence force and finally end a drawn-out war with secessionist guerrillas on Bougainville.

Singirok said in an 11-page signed statement that he believed it was morally and ethically wrong to hire the mercenaries when the money could have been used to re-equip and boost the morale of the country's own security forces. He also called for dialogue rather than confrontation with the rebels.

He said: "As a professional military officer of this country I strongly believe that what the government has decided to do is a quick-fix military solution on Bougainville and I, as the commander, am not going to play the game."

There was no immediate reaction to Singirok's move from Chan, who was elected in 1994 and faces a general election in June. Chan called an emergency cabinet meeting and was due to give a news conference later on Monday.

Singirok called on the country's governor-general to appoint a caretaker government pending an inquiry into the hiring of the mercenaries. Experts said governor-general Sir Wiwa Korowi had no constitutional power to unseat Chan.
The contract with British-based firm Sandline International, which he said was worth US$36 million for three months, had "serious negative social, security, economic and political implications".
Singirok said the defence force would no longer cooperate with the 40 foreign soldiers already on Bougainville, and Tuat said they had been detained and could be expelled.

Sandline has hired soldiers from the South Africa-based private army Executive Outcomes, including former soldiers from the white-led South African Defence Force and Nelson Mandela's African National Congress as well as other foreigners.

Papua New Guinean troops have battled for the past nine years to quell the Bougainville uprising, which led to the closure of the giant Panguna copper-gold mine, owned 53.6 percent by RTZ Corp Plc-CRA Ltd.
The mine had contributed much-needed foreign capital to Papua New Guinea, which relies on exports if crude oil, gold, timber, copper and coffee for its per capita gross domestic product of US$1,228.
Singirok also referred to what he described as speculation that the Sandline contract was related to the equipping of a private security firm owned by Chan's family.
Australia, backed by the United States and New Zealand, has vigorously opposed Chan's plans to use mercenaries.
A spokesman for Australian Prime Minister John Howard said on Monday the government was following the situation "very closely and with great concern".

Singirok's revolt hit PNG-related stocks quoted on the Australian Stock Exchange. Orogen Minerals Ltd, a mining group 51-percent owned by the PNG government, saw its shares lose nearly seven percent on the day.
